assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the final project and the final assessment to finish the course.

faq.q: Do I need a Google account?
faq.a: Not for this course: the practice labs run in GrowQR. To use the skills for real you will want a free Google Account, or a school or work account.

faq.q: Do the labs work exactly like Google's own tools?
faq.a: They work like Docs, Sheets and Slides for everything taught here: structure, formulas, formats, layouts and checks. Google's menus move from time to time, so the lessons describe what each feature is called and what it does.
About eleven and a half hours, in short sessions. Each module takes around two hours.
Finishing every module and the final assessment marks the course complete on your GrowQR profile.

activities.title: Choose the right access
activities.objective: Match each situation to the least access that gets the job done.
activities.scenario: Every file in Drive has a list of people and what each may do. Giving more access than needed is the commonest way work gets changed or leaked by accident.
steps: Read each situation.
Choose Viewer, Commenter or Editor.
Press Check my work.

checks.label: Item 1 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: They only need to read it. Viewer access cannot change anything.

checks.label: Item 2 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A commenter can leave comments and suggestions but cannot rewrite the text.

checks.label: Item 3 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: People who are building the file with you need to edit it.

checks.label: Item 4 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Suggestions let you accept or reject each change.

checks.label: Item 5 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A public notice should be read-only so nobody can alter it.

checks.label: Item 6 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: They update the numbers, so they must be able to edit.

activities.title: Write a file-naming and folder guide
activities.objective: Write a short guide with headings and a list so a team keeps Drive tidy.
activities.scenario: A student club's Drive is a mess: files called Untitled, Final, Final2 and Final FINAL. Draft a one-page guide so everyone names and stores files the same way.
steps: Give the guide a title and two headings: Names and Folders.
Under Names, write a short paragraph and a list of at least three naming rules.
Under Folders, write a short paragraph describing how folders are organised.
Bold the most important rule.

checks.label: A title that mentions Drive or files
checks.hint: Start with a title such as Our Drive guide.
checks.explain: A clear title says what the document is for.

spec.what: a title that names the guide

checks.label: At least two headings
checks.hint: Make Names and Folders headings with the paragraph style box.
checks.explain: Headings let readers jump to the part they need and build the outline.

checks.label: A list of at least three rules
checks.hint: Press the bullet-list button and write three rules.
checks.explain: Rules are easier to follow as a short list.

checks.label: At least two paragraphs of real sentences
checks.hint: Write a sentence or two under each heading.
checks.explain: A guide needs a reason as well as a rule.

checks.label: One important rule is bold
checks.hint: Select the key rule and press B.
checks.explain: Bold draws the eye to the rule that matters most.

activities.title: Turn rough notes into meeting minutes
activities.objective: Use headings, a table and a numbered list to make minutes that people will actually use.
activities.scenario: Here are rough notes from the student council meeting. Turn them into clear minutes with a title, headings, an attendance table and numbered action items.
steps: Make the first line a title and give it a larger size.
Make Attendance, Decisions and Actions into headings.
Turn the three names and roles into a table with three rows and two columns.
Turn the actions into a numbered list.
Bold the deadline line.

checks.label: The title is larger
checks.hint: Select the first line and choose a larger size or the Title style.
checks.explain: A bigger title shows what the document is.

checks.label: Three or more headings
checks.hint: Select Attendance, Decisions and Actions and apply Heading 2.
checks.explain: Real headings give structure and let people navigate.

checks.label: A table with 3 rows and 2 columns
checks.hint: Insert a table and type each name and role in a row.
checks.explain: A table lines up related facts in rows and columns.

checks.label: A numbered list of three actions
checks.hint: Select the three actions and press the numbered-list button.
checks.explain: Numbers show there are exactly three jobs and make it easy to refer to one.

checks.label: The deadline is bold
checks.hint: Select the deadline line and press B.
checks.explain: A deadline is the line people must not miss.

checks.label: The text is still there
checks.hint: Do not delete any of the notes.
checks.explain: Formatting changes how notes look, not what they say.

activities.title: Give a report a real structure
activities.objective: Replace hand-formatted lines with heading styles so the document has an outline.
activities.scenario: A report was typed with every line the same. Mark the title and the three sections as proper headings, put the findings in a list and write one summary sentence at the top.
steps: Make the first line a title.
Make Method, Findings and Recommendation into headings.
Turn the three findings into a bulleted list.
Add a one-sentence summary paragraph of at least ten words under the title.

checks.label: Four headings (title and three sections)
checks.hint: Use the paragraph style box: Title or Heading 1 for the title, Heading 2 for the sections.
checks.explain: Heading styles build the document outline and the navigation pane.

checks.label: The findings are a bulleted list of three
checks.hint: Select the three findings and press the bullet button.
checks.explain: Parallel findings read best as a list.

checks.label: A summary paragraph of at least ten words
checks.hint: Add a sentence under the title that states the main finding.
checks.explain: A summary lets a busy reader get the point first.

checks.label: The recommendation is still there
checks.hint: Do not delete the original sentences.
checks.explain: Structure should not change the content.

initial.html:
Water use at school

Method

Findings

The playground tap leaks overnight

Handwashing is the biggest single use

Recommendation

activities.title: Budget a class trip
activities.objective: Calculate costs with formulas, total them and show the split per student.
activities.scenario: A class of 25 is planning a trip. Work out each cost line, the total and what each student pays.
steps: In D2 multiply the number in B2 by the price in C2, then do the same for D3 and D4.
In D5 total the three amounts.
In D6 divide the total by the number of students in B6.
Format D5 and D6 as currency.

checks.label: D2 is the bus cost (12,000)
checks.explain: Quantity times price gives the cost of each line.

checks.label: D3 is the ticket cost (3,750)
checks.explain: 25 tickets at 150 each.

checks.label: D4 is the lunch cost (3,000)
checks.explain: 25 lunch boxes at 120 each.

checks.label: D5 is the total (18,750)
checks.hint: =SUM(D2:D4)

checks.label: D6 is what each student pays (750)
checks.explain: Divide the total by the number of students.

checks.label: D5 is formatted as currency
checks.hint: Select D5 and choose Currency.
checks.explain: Money reads better with a currency format.

activities.title: Track attendance with IF and COUNTIF
activities.objective: Flag students who are low on attendance and count them.
activities.scenario: A club records how many of 20 sessions each member attended. Anyone under 15 sessions needs a reminder.
steps: In C2 write an IF that shows Remind when B2 is below 15 and OK otherwise.
Fill C3 to C6.
In B8 count how many members need a reminder with COUNTIF.
Chart the sessions attended (names as labels) as a bar chart.

checks.label: C2 is OK for Anil
checks.hint: =IF(B2<15,"Remind","OK")
checks.explain: IF tests the sessions and chooses a word.

checks.label: C3 is Remind for Bhavna
checks.hint: Same formula with B3.
checks.explain: 12 is below 15.

checks.label: C4 is OK for Chirag (exactly 15)
checks.hint: Use < not <=.
checks.explain: Exactly 15 meets the target, so no reminder.

checks.label: B8 counts two reminders
checks.hint: =COUNTIF(C2:C6,"Remind")
checks.explain: COUNTIF counts the cells that say Remind.

checks.label: A bar chart of sessions by member
checks.hint: Use A2:A6 as labels and B2:B6 as values.
checks.explain: A bar chart compares members at a glance.

activities.title: Summarise sales with SUMIF and sort
activities.objective: Add up sales for one product with SUMIF, and sort a list from highest to lowest.
activities.scenario: A school shop logged sales. Find the total for Pens, the total for Books, and sort the log by amount, largest first.
steps: In F2 total the amount for Pen with SUMIF.
In F3 total the amount for Book with SUMIF.
Sort the sales (A2:B7) by amount, largest first.

checks.label: F2 is the Pen total (125)
checks.hint: =SUMIF(A2:A7,E2,B2:B7)
checks.explain: SUMIF adds the amounts for rows that match the product.

checks.label: F3 is the Book total (360)
checks.hint: =SUMIF(A2:A7,E3,B2:B7)
checks.explain: Change only the product cell.

checks.label: The amounts are sorted largest first
checks.hint: Select A1:B7 and sort by column B, Z to A.
checks.explain: Always sort the whole table so the rows stay together.

activities.title: A five-slide project pitch
activities.objective: Build a short, readable deck with a title slide, clear slide titles and a theme.
activities.scenario: Your team is pitching a school recycling project. Make five slides that a class can follow in two minutes.
steps: Slide 1 is a Title slide with the project name.
Add four more slides: The problem, Our idea, What we need, and Thank you.
Keep each content slide to a few short bullet points.
Choose a theme other than the default.

checks.label: Five to seven slides
checks.hint: Use Add slide to make more.
checks.explain: A two-minute pitch needs only a few slides.

checks.label: A title slide first
checks.hint: Choose the Title slide layout for slide 1.
checks.explain: The first slide names the project.

checks.label: Every slide has a title
checks.hint: Type a title on each slide.
checks.explain: Titles tell the audience where they are.

checks.label: Short, readable bullets
checks.hint: Keep to about four bullets of a few words.
checks.explain: People cannot read and listen to a wall of text.

checks.label: A theme other than the default
checks.hint: Open the theme picker and choose another.
checks.explain: A theme gives every slide the same look.

activities.title: Draw a process with shapes
activities.objective: Use shapes and arrows on a slide to show a process instead of listing it.
activities.scenario: Show how a recycled bottle gets a new life: collected, sorted, melted, made into something new. A diagram says it faster than four bullets.
steps: Make a slide titled How a bottle is reborn.
Add at least four shapes (boxes and arrows) in a row.
Keep the slide free of long text.

checks.label: A slide with the title How a bottle is reborn
checks.hint: Type the title at the top.
checks.explain: The title says what the diagram shows.

checks.label: At least four shapes
checks.hint: Use the shape button to add boxes and arrows.
checks.explain: Shapes make a process visible.

checks.label: No long text on the slides
checks.hint: Keep text short; let the shapes carry the idea.
checks.explain: A diagram works because it needs few words.

activities.title: Pick the right question type
activities.objective: Match each thing you want to ask to the Forms question type that collects clean answers.
activities.scenario: A good form makes it easy to answer and easy to analyse. The question type decides both.
steps: Read each thing you want to find out.
Choose the best question type.
Press Check my work.

checks.label: Item 1 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: One answer from a short list is multiple choice.

checks.label: Item 2 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: People may choose more than one, so use checkboxes.

checks.label: Item 3 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A rating that can be averaged is a linear scale.

checks.label: Item 4 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: An open opinion needs a free-text answer.

checks.label: Item 5 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A date question gives clean, consistent dates.

checks.label: Item 6 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: One answer from a fixed list is multiple choice.

items.text: Which one lunch break slot do you prefer?
items.why: One answer from a short list is multiple choice.

items.text: Which of these clubs would you join? (pick any)
items.why: People may choose more than one, so use checkboxes.

items.text: How useful was today's workshop, from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very)?
items.why: A rating that can be averaged is a linear scale.

items.text: What would you change about the workshop?
items.why: An open opinion needs a free-text answer.

items.text: When would you like the next meeting?
items.why: A date question gives clean, consistent dates.
One answer from a fixed list is multiple choice.

activities.title: Draft a feedback survey
activities.objective: Plan a short survey on paper before building it in Forms: a purpose, numbered questions and a thank-you.
activities.scenario: The robotics club wants feedback on its first term. Draft the survey as a document first, so you can check it before building the form.
steps: Write a title and a two-sentence introduction saying why you are asking and how long it takes.
Write at least six numbered questions, mixing multiple choice, a rating and one open question.
End with a one-line thank-you.
Make the title a heading.

checks.label: A title as a heading
checks.hint: Apply a heading style to the title.
checks.explain: A heading marks the title as the start of the document.

checks.label: An introduction of at least 20 words
checks.hint: Say why you are asking and how long it takes.
checks.explain: People answer more honestly when they know why you are asking.

checks.label: At least six numbered questions
checks.hint: Use the numbered list button and write six questions.
checks.explain: A numbered list makes questions easy to count and discuss.

checks.label: One rating question
checks.hint: Include a question such as 'Rate the club from 1 to 5'.
checks.explain: A rating can be averaged across everyone's answers.

checks.label: A thank-you
checks.hint: End with a line that thanks people.
checks.explain: Thanking people encourages them to respond next time.

activities.title: Safe or risky?
activities.objective: Spot habits that protect your account and your files, and habits that put them at risk.
activities.scenario: Cloud tools make sharing easy, which also makes mistakes easy. Sort these habits.
steps: Read each habit.
Choose Safe habit or Risky habit.
Press Check my work.

checks.label: Item 1 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: A second proof stops someone who has only your password.

checks.label: Item 2 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Anyone who gets the link can change or delete your work.

checks.label: Item 3 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: One leaked password opens every account.

checks.label: Item 4 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Removing people who no longer need access keeps files private.

checks.label: Item 5 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: It may be a fake sign-in page built to steal passwords.

checks.label: Item 6 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Version history is the safety net for accidental edits.

checks.label: Item 7 is in the right group
checks.hint: Ask what this item is mainly about, or which group it would cause trouble in.
checks.explain: Otherwise the next person can open your files.

items.text: Turning on 2-step verification for your account
items.why: A second proof stops someone who has only your password.

items.text: Sharing a file with Anyone with the link as Editor, to save time
items.why: Anyone who gets the link can change or delete your work.

items.text: Using one password for every site
items.why: One leaked password opens every account.

items.text: Reviewing who has access to a shared folder when a project ends
items.why: Removing people who no longer need access keeps files private.

items.text: Typing your password into a page you reached from an unexpected email
items.why: It may be a fake sign-in page built to steal passwords.

items.text: Using version history to restore an earlier copy after a mistake
items.why: Version history is the safety net for accidental edits.

items.text: Signing out of a shared computer when you finish
items.why: Otherwise the next person can open your files.

activities.title: Capstone: a one-page team project plan
activities.objective: Combine headings, a summary, a task table, numbered next steps and emphasis into a plan your team could share.
activities.scenario: Your team will run a school cleanliness week. Write the one-page plan you would share in Drive with the right people.
steps: A title that is a heading, and a summary paragraph of at least 25 words.
A heading called Tasks followed by a table with at least four rows and three columns (task, owner, date).
A heading called Sharing with a short paragraph saying who gets Viewer, Commenter and Editor access.
A heading called Next steps followed by a numbered list of at least three steps.
Bold the date of the final event.

checks.label: A title heading
checks.hint: Apply a heading style to the title.
checks.explain: The title opens the document.

checks.label: A summary paragraph of at least 25 words
checks.hint: Explain what the week is and why you are running it.
checks.explain: A summary lets a reader decide in seconds whether to read on.

checks.label: A Tasks section with a table of 4 rows and 3 columns
checks.hint: Insert a table with columns for task, owner and date.
checks.explain: A table keeps tasks, owners and dates lined up.

checks.label: At least three headings
checks.hint: Use headings for Tasks, Sharing and Next steps.
checks.explain: Headings make a one-page plan scannable.

checks.label: A sharing paragraph that mentions Viewer, Commenter and Editor
checks.hint: Say who gets each kind of access.
checks.explain: Deciding access in writing prevents later confusion.

spec.what: a sharing paragraph naming the access levels

checks.label: A numbered list of at least three next steps
checks.hint: Use the numbered-list button.
checks.explain: Numbered steps show the order to do things in.

checks.label: The final event date is bold
checks.hint: Select the date and press B.
checks.explain: The date everyone must remember should stand out.
